articles.title: Nafe Smallz Grand Theft Auto VI appearance has not 'sunk in'
articles.summary: Nafe Smallz says "hundreds of millions of people are going to be exposed to the song".
articles.body:
A rapper from Luton said it has "not fully sunk in" after his voice appeared on the soundtrack of Grand Theft Auto VI.

Nafe Smallz features on Personal, a track by house producer and DJ Jaden Thompson that can be heard in a nightclub in the game.

Smallz previously appeared in Grand Theft Auto V on Skepta's track Greaze Mode, which was added to the game in a 2019 update.

He said: "I don't think it's fully sunk in yet, I'm currently playing the game, I just got to Vice City in the game so I'm waiting to get to the club and hear it for myself - but yeah, it is super exciting."

Pre-orders and first-day sales of Grand Theft Auto VI totalled more than 24.5 million units , making about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics site Sensor Tower.

The previous game sold about 235 million copies and was the fastest entertainment release to reach $1bn in sales.

Although Smallz has not made it far enough into the game to hear himself, friends have sent him clips and told him the track forms part of its story mode.

He said: "At first I thought it might just be on the radio or when you're playing online, but the fact that it's actually built into the default story mode is incredible.

"It just means hundreds of millions of people are going to be exposed to the song."

Smallz, a lifelong fan of the franchise who grew up playing previous titles Vice City and San Andreas, described the placement as a "full-circle moment" as he expands into house music.

He added: "It's just showing people the range of what we could do, it's not just the rap stuff.

"It's just a blessing, you know what I'm saying?"

articles.title: Marshall amps founder, 82, says live music is still his drug
articles.summary: Terry Marshall, son of the "Father of Loud" still attends gigs and says he loves playing on stage.
articles.body:
Octogenarian Terry Marshall has no interest in stepping away from loud gigs.

While others his age might prefer peace and quiet, the Marshall Amplification co-founder still attends shows to support bands in Milton Keynes, where he lives, and jumps on stage with his saxophone whenever he gets the chance.

He said: "I say at 82, I still want to go out and get my musical fix.

"The only drug I've taken is music and I can't get away from it."

Terry founded the business with his father, Jim Marshall, who was dubbed the "Father of Loud" for creating equipment used by some of rock's biggest names.

It began as a music shop in London, but encouragement from rock'n'roll stars such as Pete Townshend of The Who led the family to start making amplifiers in the early 1960s.

Terry said: "Pete wanted something more than was available, he wanted more power.

"My father physically made the very first 4x12 cabinet. It was the first in the world, and it's been copied all over the world."

At one time The Who were listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the loudest band in concert.

Over the years, Marshall amplifiers have been used by some of music's biggest names, including Jimi Hendrix, Kurt Cobain, Oasis and Kendrick Lamar.

The amps that spoof metal band Spinal Tap used, which went up to 11 were made by you-know-who.

Marshall moved its factory to Bletchley , near Milton Keynes, in the late 1960s.

Terry recalls: "People are still using cabinets and amps we built in 1963, which is one of the greatest compliments we can get."

The company is now majority-owned by Chinese investors, but the Marshall family retains a 20% stake.

Terry has spent almost his entire life on stage. He first performed alongside his father, a drummer and singer, when he was 10 and began earning money as a musician at 14, before the family opened its shop.

His passion for music is part of the reason Marshall's factory also contains a studio where artists can record.

"I cannot walk through the factory without people stopping, shaking my hand, or giving me a hug.

"I was determined to make [the studio] an area where a musician walks in and feels comfortable, because then you get the best from them."

In 2016, the company launched Marshall Records, a label intended to build on the family's musical legacy by supporting grassroots artists.

Steve Tannett, director of music platforms at Marshall Group, started the label and said having the studio reduced the amount artists must spend hiring a recording space.

He said: "It really changed the dynamic of what I'd originally set out to do, which was much more traditional, into something that was much more artist-friendly.

"That was so exciting to see a brand and a company like Marshall willing to support artists in that way. It's very unusual."

Tannett said Marshall's historic connection to music was behind the company's determination to support artists.

Terry remains just as driven by music and has no interest in retiring anytime soon.

He said: "I'm still ambitious to play on stage; I can't get that out of my system."

articles.title: Thousands evacuated as ‘unknown substance’ fills UK arena during US rapper’s show
articles.summary: Thousands of people were evacuated after an “unknown substance” was released during a concert starring American rapper Don Toliver in the English city of Manchester on Sunday night.
articles.body: Thousands of people were evacuated after an “unknown substance” was released during a concert starring American rapper Don Toliver in the English city of Manchester on Sunday night. Plumes of smoke filled the Co-op Live arena at around 10 p.m. local time, sparking panic among the more than 12,000 revelers in the venue, footage verified by CNN shows. It triggered a major incident response and rattled nerves in the English city that was the scene of a terror attack in 2017, when a suicide bomber killed at least 22 people, including children, during an Ariana Grande concert. “It is understood that a substance believed to be tear gas was let off in the crowd towards the end of a concert,” police initially said Sunday night, but a later statement referred to an “unknown substance.” More than 50 people sought help for eye and respiratory symptoms and one person required hospital treatment, according to Manchester’s North West Ambulance Service. Concertgoer Yewande Famutimi she said suddenly felt a “burning sensation” in her throat while she was dancing. “It was very scary… We were struggling to breathe and coughing really badly,” she told CNN. “We could see people running out of the arena’s floor. We were confused whether the show would continue but once the lights turned on, we knew it was over.” Police said the arena was safely evacuated, and urged anyone “who has since noticed side effects or become ill” to visit their local hospital. Lyndsey Liverpool said it was “terrifying waiting to hear news” of her son who was celebrating his 17th birthday with friends at the event. “He said there was smoke and what looked like flares, then the lights went on and Don Toliver walked off,” Liverpool told CNN. “There was no (phone) signal to call him. It was a massive worry trying to find them.” Usman Asghar, who was at the concert, said the 23,500-capacity venue was “a complete mess” and he found it strange that security did not conduct thorough entry checks. “Security did not use metal detectors to check us, did not frisk us as usual and did not even check my wife’s bag,” Asghar told CNN. “When this incident occurred, staff told us (Don Toliver was) taking a ‘break’ and did not tell anyone what was going on. No communication with the thousands of customers.” Co-op Live did not respond to CNN’s enquiry about the security measures in place on Sunday but a spokesperson said the venue is working closely with police “to identify the cause and action appropriately.” “Our priority remains the safety and security of all visitors to Co-op Live, and we will provide more information once we have an update from (police),” the spokesperson added. CNN has contacted Don Toliver’s team for comment. Scars remain Concertgoers and others on social media, expressed how the incident instantly resurfaced the horrors of the Manchester Arena attack in the city. “This felt horrible as many of us are traumatized by the incident in 2017,” said Asghar. Liverpool said that attack was still “forefront of my mind” every time she, or her children, attended events. “We rely on these venues and the staff they employ to keep us safe and prevent issues like this from happening.” Police said enquiries are underway into what the substance is and what caused the incident. Several people were still waiting to be medically assessed overnight, the force said early Monday. “Our priority was to ensure the safety of every person that was attending the concert,” said Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker. Shortly after the incident, Co-op Live shared police updates via its X page, urging people to stay away from the arena while emergency services were helping people evacuate.

articles.title: A ban on dancing? It’s not ‘Footloose’– it’s South Korea
articles.summary: The South Korean government is considering passing a radical piece of legislation: letting people “dance freely” in restaurants that play music.
articles.body: The South Korean government is considering passing a radical piece of legislation: letting people “dance freely” in restaurants. For more than a decade, that’s been a problem for many small live music venues that have registered as general restaurants so that they can serve food and alcohol, instead of entertainment establishments, which come with stricter regulations and higher taxes. The problem: under the country’s federal Food Sanitation Act, people in restaurants don’t have what South Korean megastars BTS might call “permission to dance.” Some areas, like the Mapo-gu district of Seoul where the club-heavy neighborhood of Hongdae is located, have their own local ordinances that allow restaurants to apply for dance permits. But these are on a case-by-case basis, and only a handful of districts across the country have such ordinances. One pub and live music venue in the southeastern coastal city of Busan faced this dilemma firsthand over the summer. The venue, Ovantgarde, hosts concerts and music nights that feature musicians from across the country, playing blues to ballads to rock. But in August, they went too far—and allowed people to dance, prompting authorities to hand down a business suspension that forced it to close for two months. This might sound like something out of the 1984 classic film “Footloose” – but it’s been a pain point for many businesses and for the indie music community for years. Ovantgarde may prove to be a tipping point; after its suspension, more than 22,000 people signed a petition to the country’s legislature demanding legal change. This time, authorities appear to be listening. “At the time (of Ovantgarde’s suspension), I expressed my regret that such outdated and restrictive regulations were still in place and promised to find a solution as soon as possible,” wrote Chae Hwi-young, the Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism, in an Instagram post on Friday. Now, he said, the ministry aims to create a new business category to give “live clubs formal legal recognition” under guidelines that recognize their unique position as neither fully a restaurant nor a nightclub. That will allow live music venues to both serve food and allow customers to “dance freely,” he wrote. He added that he had personally visited Ovantgarde and met with its owner, as well as other members of the indie music community, to explain the policy proposals—which was met with an enthusiastic response. “Live clubs are incubators for emerging artists, as well as vibrant creative spaces where musicians can experiment boldly with new ideas and connect with one another,” the post said, adding that such venues must be protected for “the next generation of musicians who will shape the future of K-culture.” Many social media users rejoiced at the news, with comments under Chae’s post calling the change long overdue – especially for a country that has staked its soft power and economic success on the so-called “K-wave,” the global popularity of Korean cultural exports like K-pop, K-dramas and K-beauty. But the legal process could take many more months. The ministry must now draft a proposal, which involves consulting other government agencies, before passing it through the National Assembly legislature; the public will also have a chance to review the proposal. In the meantime, live clubs wait for their fortunes to change, and customers wait to get their groove on. Ovantgarde formally reopened in late October; attendees walking into the venue will see music posters plastered along the staircase, an elevated stage for performers at the front, and multiple signs with stark block letters that read: “NO DANCE.”

articles.title: Europe’s hot autumn of protests is a symptom of economic breakdown
articles.summary: European governments beholden to corporate interests no longer have the wellbeing of their nations as a top priority.
articles.body:
Europe is in the grips of a “hot autumn”. For several weeks now, French students have led mass protests against underinvestment in education, teacher shortages and dilapidated classrooms.

In Spain, mass protests broke out after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years, after her rent was hiked by 230 percent by an investment fund that bought the property. She died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.

Now the protests are spreading: to Italy, where upwards of one million people took to the streets of 50 cities last week; to Portugal, where tent encampments have sprung up to oppose rapid hikes in housing costs; to Germany, where riot police with water cannon confronted protesters opposing the creeping extension of conscription; and most recently, to the United Kingdom, where thousands of students joined a day of action on November 20 under the slogan “Fight for our future, not their wars!”

The common thread which has sparked these Gen Z protests is the rapidly rising cost of living. In the wake of the global pandemic, the war in Ukraine, US tariffs, and now the US-Israel war on Iran, global supply chains are breaking down, sending costs spiralling.

But this is only a symptom of a wider problem. Deregulation and neoliberal policies have allowed corporations to take over not only the economy but also politics. This has led to massive wealth concentration at the top and increasing precarity for the vast majority of the European population. The impact of climate change and the rollout of artificial intelligence (AI), threatening mass unemployment, are making the situation a lot worse.

If we want to change course, we need to fundamentally rethink how our economy works. And yet we are ruled by a political class which has lost its will to govern.

Of course, our rulers still clamour for the perks of office. But they are operating within a logic which prevents them from taking the action necessary to deal with the challenges humanity faces. In this crisis, the centre cannot hold, and support for both radical right and left-wing parties is growing rapidly.

The problem is this: 40 years ago, politicians came to accept that the free market held the answer to all our problems. Governments gave up trying to manage the economy. By handing the levers of control to the private sector, they were told they would unleash the forces of competition and economic growth, free from the sclerotic hand of the state.

As the decades wore on, it became increasingly clear that the market looked less like multiple small businesses competing for customers and more like gigantic corporations forcing citizens, governments and the planet itself to bend to their will.

Power has been handed to monopolies, which have stretched supply chains to a breaking point, privatised profits while socialising costs, fuelled inequality and trashed the environment.

Key economic decisions once made by elected governments with at least a pretence of public interest in mind are today made in corporate boardrooms, with only the self-interest of their rich investors to trouble them.

When economic decisions are designed primarily to enrich the few, is it any wonder our public infrastructure is crumbling? The things we need to make life acceptable – housing, education, healthcare – have become no more than commodities from which the monopolists can profit.

Politicians are dismantling our welfare state, claiming that today we can no longer afford to care for the poorest. They have it the wrong way around. Rather, we cannot afford the rich.

In today’s crisis, some in Europe have come to accept the need for industrial strategy, for economic planning and government intervention; all tools which were abandoned at the onset of the “free market” era.

But these tools cannot be used properly without taking power back from the monopolies – fundamentally shifting the relationship between those who now own society and those of us who live in it. It requires a New Deal at least on the scale of President Franklin D Roosevelt’s policies in the 1930s in the United States.

And in some ways, our task is even bigger today. After World War II, European politicians built a new social contract: we would all share in the massive economic growth which would be unlocked as countries recovered from war and exploited the Earth as never before. With high growth, the poor could get richer even while the rich themselves did well.

In a world facing massive resource constraints, we can no longer operate in this way. Indeed, the richest countries have already used up their fair share of global resources.

One way out is to reassert Western dominance. The one economic area in which European governments will invest is the war machine. Even Germany’s steadfast commitment to balanced budgets – a commitment which it has disastrously imposed on the European Union with almost religious zeal – can seemingly be broken when the military demands it.

But military spending will not resuscitate European industry. Nor will it keep us safe. It will further empower the monopolies who soak up ever more of our taxes while bringing catastrophic conflict ever closer. This is not protecting us from invasion but protecting Europe’s ability to do what it wants, when it wants, where it wants. We cannot, any longer, build prosperity and security on injustice. The youth protests get that; just look at the explicitly antimilitary slogans on the streets of German cities.

A real solution requires a much bigger shift in thinking. We need to accept that Europe is entering a post-growth world, where society’s resources need to be fundamentally reallocated.

This change will not be easy. It needs politicians with the will and the ability to remove power from the corporations, to break up monopoly capitalism. And that will not come from above because, as American statesman Frederick Douglass said: “power concedes nothing without a demand”.

Europe’s youth demand radical change. Hope lies with them.

articles.title: Delta automation system issue fixed but delays remain ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.summary: Over 1,000 Delta flights were delayed Sunday after an automated system that calculates an aircraft’s weight malfunctioned during a busy time for travel ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
articles.body: Over 1,000 Delta flights were delayed Sunday after an automated system that calculates an aircraft’s weight malfunctioned during a busy time for travel ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The airline said Sunday morning that its teams were using manual workarounds to get flights off the ground while they sought to restore the automation system that ensures an aircraft isn’t too heavy to fly. Hours later, Delta said that system was once again working, though flights were still not back to normal. The airline said it was helping passengers who needed hotel rooms or meals but hoped to have all the delayed flights in the air by the end of the day. On Sunday morning, the Federal Aviation Administration issued about an hourlong ground stop to some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, which is Delta’s hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. Complying with the weight and balance limits of an aircraft is critical to flight safety, according to an FAA document, and going above the limit can compromise the structural integrity of the aircraft. The agency said on X that the delays were not related to FAA air traffic systems. Earlier this month, a malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers canceled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days after that, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights. The Delta delays come as Americans have been encountering a growing number of problems with technology that are increasingly disrupting their lives. And the disruptions came just days before the Thanksgiving holiday, the busiest travel season in the United States. As of Sunday evening, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 58%, or about 2,000, of Delta’s flights were delayed; it wasn’t immediately clear how many of those involved flights into or out of the Atlanta airport. FlightAware said that about 58% of flights out of the Atlanta airport were delayed while about 50% of flights destined for the airport were delayed. The vast majority of flights at the Atlanta airport are operated by Delta. Delta said about 70% of the delays and cancellations noted by FlightAware were connected to the automation issue and the rest were because of inclement weather. By mid-afternoon Delta was apologizing for the delays, and said it was rebooking customers and providing meals and hotel rooms where needed, and offering refunds if a flight was canceled. articles.title: For centuries, there were rumors of tunnels under this 1,500-year-old landmark. Now they’ve been found
articles.summary: A network of newly discovered tunnels and underground spaces, some hundreds of meters long, has been excavated under the Hagia Sophia Grand Mosque in Istanbul, with more expected to be be revealed.
articles.body: A network of newly discovered tunnels and underground spaces, some hundreds of meters long, has been excavated under the Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, with yet more expected to be revealed. It’s a highly significant discovery at one of the world’s most popular UNESCO World Heritage sites, a magnificent sixth-century megastructure that was built as a church over a Roman temple, and was subsequently converted into a mosque and then a museum. Since 2020, it has been used as a mosque once more. Today’s building, the fourth place of worship on the site after the temple and two previous churches, was built in 537 CE. However, sections of the hidden world now being uncovered are believed to predate even that, Turkey’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced Friday. Last year saw the start of a three-year conservation project at the Hagia Sophia, which will restore its central dome and improve the building’s already impressive earthquake resilience, having outlasted both the Eastern Roman (or Byzantine) and Ottoman empires. These are the most comprehensive works at the site in nearly 1,500 years of history. Rumors about hidden tunnels underneath the Hagia Sophia have persisted for centuries, and underground infrastructure, including a four-room Roman hypogeum, or burial structure, was discovered in the 1940s. In early 2025, during cleaning work in the vaulted cellars forming the basement level of what was once the Hagia Sophia’s atrium courtyard, previously unknown subterranean structures were uncovered. Nearly 3,000 tons cleared so far Since then, work has been underway to clean, document and preserve the spaces. These include tunnels, water channels, vaulted chambers, a burial structure and a passage that is believed to be linked to a fifth-century Roman street. The cleaning process has been documented step by step using terrestrial laser scanning and, as it progresses further, “the infrastructural system of this unique world heritage monument will be revealed in its entirety,” Hasan Fırat Diker, from the Hagia Sophia Scientific Committee, wrote in a study in March 2026. Nearly 3,000 tons of debris have so far been removed from the underground infrastructure and 420 meters of tunnels have already been cleared (around a quarter of a mile). They may extend for kilometers more. Minister of Culture and Tourism Mehmet Nuri Ersoy inspected the site and spoke to the media in an announcement on November 20. “Throughout history, this underground network has served important functions in water distribution and the drainage of rainwater,” Ersoy said in a translated statement. “Through our work, as we uncover Hagia Sophia’s underground structures, we are also deepening our knowledge of Istanbul’s historic water management infrastructure.” Layers of history So far, six chambers have been discovered, connected by nine tunnels. Nearly 600 feet (180 meters) has been cleared in the longest of the tunnels. “We think this line may be associated with a Roman road. It runs parallel to Hagia Sophia’s entrance façade, starting in front of the Fatih Madrasa and extending towards the visitor entrance,” said Ersoy. The Roman hypogeum, or burial structure, is underneath the area of the Hagia Sophia known as the Vizier’s Garden. Cleaning work there led the team five feet below the mud-covered floor. “We believe this section dates from a period earlier than the present Hagia Sophia structure,” said Ersoy. “In this way, we are also bringing to light the building layers beneath the monument that span different periods.” Alongside the conservation and documentation work, the goal is to “make Hagia Sophia’s underground historical riches visible” by opening suitable sections to the public, Ersoy said, although no timeline for this has been announced. This “would be one of the most remarkable developments in Istanbul’s cultural tourism in recent years,” says historian and tour guide Hasan Barış Partal. “Beneath this magnificent monument ıies another fascinating story of Imperial Constantinople,” as Istanbul was then known, and “the city’s extensive freshwater supply network.” These underground waterways could potentially have been connected to the great aqueducts of the ancient city, he says, and offer intriguing evidence of Constantinople’s remarkable engineering achievements. “I believe that walking through these underground spaces could evoke a feeling similar to descending into the Vatican Grottoes beneath St. Peter’s Basilica, where many popes are buried,” says Partal. “Although their historical functions are very different, both offer the extraordinary experience of discovering another world beneath an iconic monument.” The current Hagia Sophia was built on the orders of Emperor Justinian I, when Constantinople was the heart of the Eastern Roman Empire. It was preceded by two earlier churches on the site, which were themselves built over a pagan temple. During its five-year construction, from 523 CE, Justinian instructed his provincial governors to send the choicest artifacts from ancient ruins in their territories to Constantinople for use in the Hagia Sophia. Buildings costs were said to reach around $75 million, equivalent to $1.3 billion today. Ali Halit Diker contributed to this report.

articles.title: San Francisco braces for near-record tides as a storm collides with Thanksgiving travel‌
articles.summary: San Francisco Bay could rise to near-record levels this week, as a strong storm coupled with some of the year’s highest tides moves ashore, threatening to flood city streets and a major West Coast airport on some of the busiest travel days of the year.
articles.body: San Francisco Bay could rise to near-record levels this week, as a strong storm coupled with some of the year’s highest tides moves ashore, threatening to flood city streets and a major West Coast airport on some of the busiest travel days of the year. 🌧️ Track the storm in the CNN Weather app The National Weather Service issued a rare coastal flood warning for Monday through Thanksgiving Day, with peak flooding around each morning’s high tide, and the highest water expected Wednesday. As holiday flyers fill airports this week, travel disruptions are a key concern. San Francisco International Airport, which had more than 1.8 million passengers pass through its gates in the 12 days around Thanksgiving last year, and Oakland-San Francisco Bay Airport, which expects about 250,000, both sit on low-lying land right along the bay. Water levels may reach as much as 2.8 feet above a normal high tide, approaching the record set in 1983, Dylan Flynn, a lead meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s San Francisco Bay Area office, told CNN. “Another storm, a cold front, is coming that’s stronger than what we dealt with last couple days … on top of king tides, on top of El Niño, all of that bumps the water level up,” Flynn said, adding Thanksgiving week “just happens to be unfortunately lining up with the highest tides we’ve seen in 40 years.” Airports prepare for bad weather, high water Arriving at the airport could be its own challenge. “Just getting there, driving through roads, we expect numerous road closures,” Flynn said. “The airports have taken a lot of mitigation efforts to stop the flooding but San Francisco and Oakland International are both low-lying infrastructure,” Flynn said. “So without those mitigations, they would have tidal flooding.” Forecasters are in regular contact with both airports’ emergency operations centers whenever heavy rain, flooding, strong winds or high tides are expected, he added. The airports have known about this week’s king tides “well in advance,” he said. “They’re well prepared.” “While we don’t know exactly what conditions might materialize, we are prepared to address any flooding issues that might arise,” San Francisco International spokesperson Doug Yakel told CNN. “SFO facilities staff have already ensured drainage areas are clear and pump stations are in top operating condition. Facilities staff will continue to monitor storm drains and airfield drainage outfall pipes to keep them free from debris and obstructions, and engineers will monitor pump stations to ensure they remain functional and have backup portable pumps ready to deploy as needed.” The airport has also staged sandbags and portable flood barriers in high-risk areas, including locations susceptible to flooding and locations where stormwater runoff could affect airport operations. “The SFO Airside Operations team will conduct regular inspections of the airfield perimeter, taxiways, runways and vehicle service roads to identify any flooding or standing water and will coordinate alternatives as needed,” Yakel said. Oakland-San Francisco Bay Airport recently finished raising and seismically reinforcing its perimeter dike, which protects the airport’s primary runway, airport public information officer Kaley Skantz said in a statement to CNN. Ahead of this week’s tides, the airport serviced and tested its airfield pump systems, Skantz said. Airport crews and the cities of Oakland and Alameda have also cleared storm lines, and sandbags are in place in critical areas. “Our OAK team is experienced in doing this kind of preparation,” Skantz said. Travelers should be able to get there, too, according to the airport. The two most-used routes in and out, Hegenberger Road and 98th Avenue, “do not face risk of tidal flooding,” Skantz said, and the airport is advising passengers to use them. CNN has reached out to the Federal Aviation Administration for comment. How the city is preparing San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie warned an “extremely serious” situation was about to hit the city and urged residents to rethink their holiday plans. “I know there’s a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday, but I’m going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential starting Monday afternoon and going into Wednesday afternoon,” Lurie said in a video posted to Instagram. As of Monday, Forecasters are expecting water levels to reach 8.6 feet during Wednesday morning’s high tide. City officials are preparing for tides exceeding 9 feet, Lurie said. “We could see water at Ocean Beach reach all the way to the seawall.” The National Weather Service issued a high surf warning for Wednesday along the Pacific coast, including San Francisco’s Ocean Beach, where 20- to 30-foot breaking waves could sweep people off the beach and into the ocean. Lurie said the city is opening its emergency operations center, with crews out “every single day going forward.” The Port of San Francisco is deploying flood barriers and pumps along the waterfront. The San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency is preparing for disruptions to transit and traffic across the city, particularly along the Embarcadero. The Department of Emergency Management is coordinating preparations among city and state agencies. City workers handed out 10,000 sandbags in a single day at a giveaway where residents waited in long lines, Lurie said. Crews worked from 5 a.m. until about 4 p.m. “I know people have been waiting in line for a long time. I appreciate San Franciscans preparing,” he said. The mayor urged residents not to drive through floodwater, to stay out of the water and away from beaches, and to sign up for emergency alerts from AlertSF by texting their ZIP code to 888-777. Waymo has proactively paused service across the Bay Area. The company said it will monitor roadways through the week and “gradually resume commercial ride-hailing services once conditions improve.” The US Coast Guard’s Sector San Francisco warned in a video posted to Facebook the tides could run 1 to 2 feet above normal and higher with storm surge, the highest predicted in 18 years. It said people near the San Francisco waterfront, in Marin and San Mateo counties, or along any low-lying bay shoreline should expect flooding on coastal roads, bike paths and beach parking lots. It recommended boat owners check mooring lines, dock cleats and waterfront gear. Beachgoers should stay off jetties and rocks and watch for sneaker waves. Never drive through standing water, it added, because depth is deceptive, and saltwater can quickly ruin a car. Another round of high tides is expected December 22 through 25, which the Coast Guard expects to be the highest of the season, followed by January 20 through 23. That’s where climate change comes in, Flynn said. Sea level is rising about 2 millimeters a year near San Francisco. “It’s not very much year to year,” he said, but over the more than 40 years since the 1983 record, it adds up to several inches. “So it doesn’t take quite as strong of a storm to get the same water level,” Flynn said. “If we get a strong storm like we had in 1983 with these baseline water levels, it would be much, much worse.” Flynn expects the record, set in January 1983, to hold, though the water could come close. “We probably won’t break that record. We’ll be close,” he said. The 1983 record “took an exceptionally strong storm to get those water levels. … That was the worst-case scenario.” A storm, a king tide and El Niño on top of rising seas No single force is driving this week’s threat, Flynn said. A cold front stronger than the storms of the past few days is arriving at the same time as king tides, the highest tides of the year. Both come on top of El Niño, which has already pushed water levels up. “When you stack those three or four things on top of each other, we’re going to see tides that we really rarely ever see,” he said. El Niño alone accounts for about a foot of the extra water, according to Flynn. Water off the coast is in the mid-60s, about 10 degrees above normal. Warmer water expands, “and the only place it can go is up,” he said. Since early October, tides have been running at least a foot above predictions and more than 2 feet higher during some storms. The incoming storm should add roughly another 6 inches. “I’ll be honest: This is not the strongest storm in the world. This is not worst-case scenario. It just happens to line up with king tide,” Flynn said. “No one of these factors is super critical. They’re just all stacking up on top of each other to bring us this near-record flooding.” Who should be worried How much it matters depends on where you are, Flynn said. Residents in low-lying areas along the bay shore, especially on the city’s east and northeast sides, should take the warning seriously. “If you know that you flood or get close to flooding during king tides, this is going to be worse than a normal king tide by up to a foot or a foot and a half,” he said. “Now, if you’re inland, even just a few blocks inland, you might not even notice.” His advice: Know when high tide is, stay away from low-lying infrastructure, and move your car if you live or work near the water. CNN Meteorologist Briana Waxman contributed to this report.

articles.title: Why is Bangladesh’s Grameen Bank under attack?
articles.summary: Leading financial institution has found itself at centre of tensions amid violence by Sheikh Hasina supporters.
articles.body:
Dhaka, Bangladesh – When attackers stormed a Grameen Bank branch in Kashiani last week, they did not just damage furniture and equipment. They also destroyed records accumulated over nearly three decades.

Solaiman Morol, the branch manager in Bangladesh’s Gopalganj district, said about a dozen men arrived on the afternoon of November 18 carrying machetes, petrol and tools to break the locks. Staff members were away on field visits.

The attackers looted the branch and tried to cut open its vault with a grinder. They took out about 40 sacks of vouchers and other documents and set them on fire. They also looted steel cupboards, filing cabinets, chairs, tables and other equipment. A staff member’s rice cooker was among the items taken away. “They said that after burning the records, nobody would have to repay their loans,” Morol said.

Videos of the attack later appeared online. Morol said he heard slogans including “Joy Bangla” and “Joy Bangabandhu”, associated with ousted former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina ’s Awami League, as well as calls to burn what the attackers described as “Yunus’s den”.

The branch has not been able to resume normal operations. Staff members have received threats and customers are worried about the safety of their deposits and loan records.

“A bank depends on trust. This is impacting our customers’ confidence. People who have deposits with us are becoming frightened,” Morol said.

The attack was part of a wider wave of violence against Grameen Bank. Its latest internal memorandum, dated November 23, records 97 attacks on branches and offices between November 10 and 23.

The attacks have put the Nobel Prize-winning institution founded by Muhammad Yunus at the centre of Bangladesh’s political tensions, months after he stepped down as chief adviser following Hasina’s removal from power in August 2024. Hasina supporters set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members in Faridpur and Narail.

In a statement on Monday, Yunus called “the systematic assault” on Grameen Bank “unbelievably shocking”, noting that bank officials and borrower-members “narrowly escaped fatal injury” in several incidents.

Grameen Bank is one of Bangladesh’s best-known financial institutions. It pioneered a model of microcredit that provides small loans to people who often cannot access conventional banking services.

About 90 percent of its ownership belongs to its borrower-members, while the government holds the remaining 10 percent. It has around 10.6 million members, most of them rural women, according to its managing director, Sarder Akhter Hamed. Around 5.5 million borrowers have outstanding loans worth more than Tk19,000 crore ($1.53bn). Members also hold deposits of around Tk25,000 crore ($2bn) with the bank.

“There are many people in the communities we serve whom other banks and financial institutions are unwilling to lend to. We stand beside them and provide access to credit,” Hamed said.

The attacks have disrupted the bank’s work and left staff members worried about their safety. Hamed said the institution has around 21,000 employees and that the violence had affected them psychologically. “There is a sense of insecurity,” he said.

Is the Awami League targeting Grameen Bank – and why?

The government has blamed the Awami League, the party of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, for the attacks.

“The government is making every effort to maintain law and order,” Ziauddin Ahmed, additional secretary in charge of the political wing at the Ministry of Home Affairs, told Al Jazeera.

The attacks come amid renewed political activity by Hasina’s supporters, which has led to serious unrest in parts of the country, for example Gopalganj, her ancestral district. Hasina supporters have set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members.

Political analysts say Grameen Bank has become a symbol through which some Awami League supporters can direct their anger at Yunus, under whose interim rule Hasina’s party was banned from electoral politics. During Yunus’s stint as Bangladesh’s leader, Hasina was also convicted by a tribunal for massacres carried out against protesters who challenged her rule in 2024. Hasina faces a death sentence, but has recently asserted that she intends to return to Bangladesh from India , where she has lived in exile since she was ousted.

Mubashar Hasan, a researcher at the humanitarian and development research initiative at Western Sydney University, said the timing was significant.

“Her party has spent the week pushing for her return. Grameen Bank is the easiest symbol of Dr Yunus they can reach,” he said. “For the Awami League’s hardliners, Yunus is the face of their fall, so burning his bank is a way of hitting back at him.”

The attacks, Hasan argued, may also be intended to demonstrate that the party still has a presence on the streets, despite the ban. “Some of these attacks look like a performance of strength, especially in Gopalganj, to tell supporters ‘we are still here’,” he said.

Asif Mohammad Shahan, a professor in the department of development studies at the University of Dhaka, sees the violence as part of a broader political strategy .

He said the Awami League had two possible routes after the August 2024 uprising: acknowledge its mistakes and seek political rehabilitation, or try to force its way back into politics. In his assessment, the party has chosen the latter.

“The attack on Grameen Bank is actually an effort of sending a message of ‘politics of revenge’,” Shahan said.

He said the attacks could also be intended to provoke the government into a heavy-handed response, allowing the party to portray itself as a victim and challenge the government’s legitimacy.

Why is Grameen Bank particularly vulnerable, and who is paying the price?

The bank’s ownership structure makes the attacks especially consequential. Most of its shares belong to the poor women who depend on it for loans, savings and other financial services.

“When a branch burns, it’s their loan files, savings records and repayment schedules going up in smoke,” Hasan of Western Sydney University said.

He warned that disruption could push borrowers towards informal lenders and make it harder for them to continue their repayment cycles.

The damage is already affecting the bank’s operations. Hamed, the Grameen Bank managing director, said the institution had suspended the accrual of interest on outstanding loans at branches unable to operate because of the attacks.

The bank is also trying to protect its staff and property. Some branches have increased security and moved staff from locations considered particularly risky.

But the consequences extend beyond damaged buildings and lost records: At stake is also the confidence of customers in the bank.

Why is the BNP government struggling to stop the attacks?

The attacks have also raised questions about the ability of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government to maintain law and order.

Ahmed, the Home Ministry official, said “it would be wrong to say that the government is struggling to contain the situation”. Police headquarters told Al Jazeera that eight cases had been filed and eight people arrested in connection with the attacks. “The problem is that our police force is somewhat short of manpower,” Ahmed said.

Shahan said the government’s response was being constrained by the knowledge that a tough crackdown could give the Awami League the chance to play victim. “The Awami League is baiting the government into attacking it so that it can quickly switch to playing the victim and try to delegitimise the government,” he said.

Hamed said police had responded whenever the bank sought help and in some cases had provided advance warnings about possible attacks. “For the most part, however, we have had to remain alert and protect ourselves,” he said.

“If the law-and-order situation in the country improves, confidence and trust [in the bank, too] will automatically return,” he said.

articles.title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship off Libya in latest expansion of the war
articles.summary: Ukraine has taken its fight against Russia to the shores of North Africa, claiming to have sunk a warship off the coast of Libya in its latest expansion of the war.
articles.body: Ukraine has taken its fight against Russia to the shores of North Africa, claiming to have sunk a warship off the coast of Libya in its latest expansion of the war. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Ukrainian naval drones had been used in the attack in the Mediterranean a day earlier, which came after Moscow said another of its ships was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea. Zelenskyy shared footage of the attacks in a post on X, showing drones approaching several vessels followed by massive fireballs. He said his forces deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones to sink the Russian corvette, Merkury, and hit a transport ship, the Angara, in an “exemplary Ukrainian operation.” Ukraine’s Security Service, SBU, said the attacks took place near the Libyan port of Benghazi, some 1,500 miles from the established front lines of the conflict. It said the corvette “regularly escorted enemy naval convoys” and in particular guarded the Angara cargo ship that was used to move weapons. “Both vessels were legitimate military targets for Ukraine, as they worked directly for Russia’s military capabilities,” the SBU said in a statement on Telegram. Ukrainian uncrewed boats were delivered to a designated location and launched into the water from a so-called “mother ship,” the SBU said, reaching their targets despite “enemy’s attempts to destroy the Ukrainian drones from the air.” It said the Ka-27 multi-purpose helicopter was on board the corvette and was also sunk. “The Defence Forces of Ukraine have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea,” the SBU added. Ukraine noted that the ship was one of Russia’s newest, commissioned only in 2023. Moscow has noted Zelenskyy’s “statement on this matter,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday when asked about the attacks. He deferred to the Russian Defense Ministry, which was yet to comment. It’s the latest example of Kyiv launching surprise attacks to hit back against the Kremlin. But the weekend attack caused fallout in Libya, where local authorities expressed outrage and the United Nations called for an independent probe. The eastern Libya-based government said Sunday that an explosion took place aboard a Russian vessel docked at the Benghazi naval base. It said the vessel was en route back to Russia and had stopped at the port to refuel and take on supplies. A comprehensive investigation into the attack will be launched, it said, in coordination with Russian authorities. “The Government views the targeting of a vessel within a Libyan port as a serious assault on national sovereignty and a blatant violation of port security and the safety of maritime navigation,” the statement added, without calling out Kyiv directly but adding that Libya was not a party to the war in Ukraine. Libya has been divided since an uprising toppled longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi in 2011. A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration with ties to Russia is located in the east of the oil-rich nation. The eastern Libya-based government has cooperation agreements and maritime facility arrangements with Russia, but Ukrainian forces also operate in the country’s west under a deal believed to be endorsed by Kyiv’s global allies. The U.N. Support Mission in Libya called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation” into the ship attack. The western Libya government expressed concerns about “dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts,” in an apparent reference to Russia’s war in Ukraine. “The government reaffirms its categorical rejection of turning Libya into an arena for international conflicts or a theater for external powers to settle scores,” it said in a statement. It’s not the first attack linked to the Ukraine war in the Mediterranean this year. Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya struck a Russian tanker in a suspected sea drone attack near Maltese waters, Libyan officials said in March. The latest attack off the coast of North Africa come just a day after a Russian-owned cargo ship was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea. The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, raising fears that the conflict is increasingly spilling over. Kyiv has not claimed responsibility, and the Ukrainian Defense Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NBC News. Peskov called the attack on Sparta II “a very dangerous trend of expanding terrorist activity in the Baltic region” Monday. The escalation in international waters comes just days after the three-way summit between the leaders of Russia, China and the U.S., during which President Donald Trump called Russian President Vladimir Putin his “friend” and said Putin wanted to end his war in Ukraine. Zelenskyy told NBC News ahead of the Shenzhen summit that he saw no signs Putin was ready for peace.

articles.body:
The House Select Committee on China may be coming to an end with Democrats taking over the House majority in January.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to be the next Speaker of the House, is ultimately responsible for whether the committee continues or is disbanded.

He says discussions about its fate won’t happen in earnest until after Democrats choose their leadership team.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the likely incoming chair of the House Foreign Affairs panel, told The Hill that his committee is capable of taking over the select panel’s responsibilities.

“We have the ability to do it. We’re ready to do it. We’ll do it. But I’ll follow the leader,” he told The Hill.

Supporters of the select committee, formally known as the Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, say the panel established by the GOP House in 2023 is the best venue for bipartisan cooperation on confronting Beijing.

But Democrats on the Foreign Affairs Committee are itching to take the lead on investigations and legislation that the select committee has overseen. They are particularly interested in focusing on President Trump’s dealings with China, including the fallout from allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — a close adviser to Trump — had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and tech business partner.

Democrats are also probing whether the administration prized profits over national security and allowed China in the process to illegally access advanced U.S. technology.

“We’ve got great talent on our committee,” Meeks told The Hill. “First we’ve got to see what the next Speaker is going to say. Once he makes his decision then we’ll plan accordingly.”

The Foreign Affairs panel has two subcommittees focused on Asia: one on East Asia and the Pacific and one on South and Central Asia. Meeks said he’s likely to overhaul the panel’s subcommittees in the new Congress.

“All of those committees, I’ve got to decide what I’m going to do – those committees were set up by the Republicans. They might not be the same committees once I make my determination,” he said.

Rep. Brad Sherman (D-Calif.), a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, sees that committee as “well-positioned to conduct oversight of the administration’s China policy.”

Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), a member of the Select Committee on China and its initial ranking member, told The Hill the panel is “absolutely” essential to combat escalating challenges from Beijing.

“Now, in the face of the CCP [Chinese Communist Party] relentlessly kind of promulgating aggression toward us, whether it’s technologically, militarily, or economically — as we just saw with Jensen Huang and Nvidia — I feel like we need to stand firm on a bipartisan basis, and bicameral basis in holding the CCP at bay,” he said.

“I’m very concerned about this CCP having gained an advantage at our expense, especially through the Jensen Huang affair, but also through other actions that the administration has taken.”

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who now serves as the ranking member of the China Select Committee, told The Hill he believes there will be an “independent committee” and said, “We’re having the conversation of what that committee looks like.”

In 2023, Jeffries gave the blessing to establish the committee in agreement with then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.).

It was a rare area of bipartisanship amid deep divisions over how the U.S. should deal with China after Democrats in 2020 boycotted a Republican “China Task Force” initiative.

When the select committee was established, Republicans were lashing out at then-President Biden for allowing a Chinese spy balloon to traverse the U.S. before shooting it down. And anti-Asian hate was still at an all-time high, tied to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Three years later, the select committee’s supporters argue the panel has demonstrated bipartisan cooperation and delivered important legislation addressing competition between the U.S. and China.

Wins, they say, include the committee advancing a bipartisan bill to force the social media app TikTok to separate from its Chinese owners.

In 2024, it produced a report detailing how the Chinese government incentivized the production of fentanyl precursor chemicals even as Beijing had agreed to stem exports. The Biden administration pushed Beijing to crack down on production and chemical exports. The Chinese government declared fentanyl a “U.S. problem.”

Other legislative wins that supporters promote include the Biosecure Act, which became law in 2025. The law calls for identifying risky foreign biotechnology companies, largely from China, and barring U.S. companies from contracting with them.

The law is intended to protect Americans’ health data and safeguard sensitive U.S. technology from, in particular, the Chinese military.

Earlier this month, the select committee released a report outlining the dangers of American companies relying on Chinese artificial intelligence models. The Trump administration is reportedly considering forcing U.S. companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI models.

“For nearly four years the Select Committee has brought together Republicans and Democrats to address the grave threats the Chinese Communist Party poses to U.S. interests and values,” Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), the outgoing chair of the select committee, said in a statement urging its renewal.

“The challenges we face as a nation are only becoming more urgent given the high-stakes technology competition in AI and the CCP’s growing coercion targeting America’s allies and partners. The coming two years will be a critical period—and an opportunity to meet the moment through the Select Committee’s bipartisan mandate and work.”

The committee could be slimmed down but shouldn’t be eliminated, argued Rush Doshi, who served as deputy senior director for China and Taiwan on the National Security Council under Biden. Doshi said Democrats should take advantage of the committee to put forth their vision for U.S.-China relations.

“Congress has other committees. But each covers a small slice of China policy,” he wrote on social platform X , alongside an analysis calling for the select committee’s renewal.

“Only the Select Committee can pull that together and balance the executive branch’s dominance of the issue. As Trump meets [Chinese President] Xi [Jinping] and [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, and as the Nvidia scandal spirals, now is the wrong time to shut down the Committee but the right time to reframe it,” wrote Doshi, a senior fellow for Asia studies and director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations.

A former committee staffer, who asked for anonymity to protect their work, described the select committee as a unique venue that helped push other House committees to look at issues linked to Chinese threats. The former staffer said its staff were given a long leash to explore ideas and propose solutions.

“They allowed us to develop ideas, produce work products and deliver results, and that’s wonderful,” the former staffer said.

“I appreciate the time when I was on the committee, I could venture out, identify a problem, sit down, do my research, and do a bill, or oversight, and create impact. In that regard I’m very grateful to our members and our senior staff for their support.”

articles.title: LSU spent $150 million on Lane Kiffin and a new roster, it finished worse than under Brian Kelly | Ian Miller
articles.summary: LSU football spent nearly $150 million on Lane Kiffin, but a loss to Tennessee dropped the Tigers to 6-5 and worse than any full Brian Kelly season.
articles.body: In the real world, early September was not so long ago. In the world of modern college football, it's been an eternity. Just a few months ago, the UCLA Bruins were a punchline, not a contender to win the Big Ten Conference and potentially secure a first round bye in the College Football Playoff. The Ohio State Buckeyes were widely viewed as the best team in the country, thanks to quarterback Julian Sayin and elite talent on defense. Then, there's the LSU Tigers. LSU'S $40 MILLION FOOTBALL ROSTER MAY HAVE BEEN A MIRAGE, ACCORDING TO CFB EXPERT JOSH PATE The Tigers made the biggest splash of the 2025-2026 offseason by hiring Lane Kiffin from Ole Miss to revitalize their program after firing Brian Kelly. Kiffin commanded an exorbitant salary, with nearly $100 million in guarantees. He hired the most expensive support staff in the country, with over $14 million in assistant salaries. They revamped the roster too, putting together massive NIL deals and the No. 1 transfer portal class, with an estimated cost of around $40-50 million. Then, week one. And boy, did it look like their decision-making had panned out. The Tigers beat Clemson 51-10 in a game that wasn't even that close. It was a complete demolition, and seemed to validate hiring Kiffin and their roster-building process. Kiffin even gave a typically sarcastic comment after the game, referencing the SEC's push to stop them from rostering players who'd formerly gone pro. With a 31-3 lead at halftime, Kiffin told ESPN's Holly Rowe, "Imagine if we'd had pro players." Essentially, "look how good we are already, we didn't even need them." Fast-forward two months, and it turns out LSU might have needed them. Badly. LANE KIFFIN TAKES THE SIDE EXIT AS TENNESSEE SENDS LSU HOME AND MOVES TO THE DOORSTEP OF CFP The Tigers' loss to the Tennessee Volunteers in Knoxville put a final nail in the coffin of a dismal season. Yes, LSU will beat up on hapless Arkansas this weekend, but every single outcome that looked possible after that Clemson game has now officially fallen by the wayside. LSU have had a difficult schedule, one of the toughest in the country, in fact, but managed to get the least out of it. There was the emotionally charged return to Oxford against Ole Miss, which it lost. It lost at Kentucky. Then it was blown out at home by Alabama. It had a late lead against Texas, only to give up a devastating touchdown to Arch Manning and Raleek Brown for another loss. On Saturday, Tennessee simply dominated the LSU offense. A whopping eight sacks, 10 tackles for loss, and just 43 rushing yards allowed on 34 attempts. It was an ugly game with six combined turnovers, and Tennessee was fortunate to cross 100 passing yards, but once again, the Tigers came up on the wrong side of what should have been a competitive game. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Winning all five of these games against solid teams might have been too much to ask for any team, but elite programs could and would expect to win some of them. LSU won none. Just 3-5 in the SEC, with the three wins coming over a woeful Texas A&M team, Mississippi State without Kamario Taylor, and Auburn. After all that talk, all the money, all the swagger and arrogance, they sit here in late November at 6-5 with one of the most disappointing seasons by any team in recent memory. And maybe even more frustrating, it's worse off than any full season under Brian Kelly. Kelly went 10-4 in 2022, 6-2 in the SEC. He went 10-3 in 2023, once again 6-2 in the SEC. He was 9-4 in 2024 and 5-3 in the SEC. Then was 5-3 when fired during the 2025 season. So in three full seasons in Baton Rouge, Kelly lost seven games, total, in the SEC, with a 17-7 overall record. Kiffin's lost five of his first eight. LANE KIFFIN BLAMES LSU'S $40+ MILLION ROSTER AFTER LOSS TO TEXAS: 'WE'LL HAVE BETTER ROSTERS’ $150 million, plus a $54 million buyout to Kelly, and they lost more SEC games in eight weeks than Kelly lost in two seasons. Maybe even more frustrating, and damning for Kiffin, is that the Tigers, by computer models based on offensive, defensive and special teams efficiency, would still be expected to play like one of the top-15 teams in the country. Their losses, at least some of them, have been a result of not making plays when it matters, or getting hurt by costly mistakes. Like, say, 16 penalties for 98 yards against Tennessee. Some of that falls on the $150 million coaching staff. Hard to get worse than that. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER What's more incredible, even, is that this is who the Tigers are, and what the program has been. After the 2019 national championship winning team with Joe Burrow, it has been comparable to a mid-tier Big Ten program by most metrics: Minnesota. And yeah, that's really close. Despite Minnesota having far fewer resources available to them. Some of this comes down to LSU playing tougher schedules; it's had 29 games against AP ranked teams compared to 19 for Minnesota, but it's won a lower percentage of those matchups, implying either a talent or coaching gap between them and their opponents. It's hard to believe, but LSU just hasn't been the type of program that they, or many fans, think they are. Maybe Kiffin's second season in Baton Rouge will be different; they'll still have a big recruiting class, transfer portal group, and plenty of money. But spending $200 million, between coaches, players, and buyouts, and finishing 6-5? Even with underlying performance suggesting a top-15 team? That's about as bad as it gets.

articles.title: The Ukraine-Russia war is seeping out across Europe and there are two reasons it will get worse
articles.summary: Rather than peace, there is stark escalation.
articles.body: Rather than peace, there is stark escalation. That is the product of over six weeks of shuttling diplomacy, posturing, betrayal of Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, Russian intransigence and the US’ failed reframing of the process as about European security and participation. Put aside the near-zero public results from the Shenzhen trilateral meeting between Russia, China and the US, and consider the violence of the past week alone. Russia launched Friday what Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky called the most intense attack of the year – a six-hour crescendo of drones and missiles, after weeks of striking Kyiv’s bridges, and power infrastructure across the country. Dozens have died, and swaths of the country and capital are often in blackout. Ukraine struck Vladimir Putin’s prized bridge to occupied Crimea three times, in the days around the trilateral. And compounding that display of technical prowess, Kyiv’s drones apparently struck both a Russian-military linked ship this weekend off the coast of Kaliningrad, and then Russian naval assets near the port of Benghazi, on the Libyan coast. Where Moscow parades its brutal, relentless intensity, Kyiv strikes back with unexpected reach and precision. Widening theater of conflict The geography of Ukrainian strikes is important. Kaliningrad is a Russian enclave between Lithuania and Poland, hitherto considered safe – an odd legacy of the Soviet era, territory marooned in the heart of some of NATO’s most anti-Russian members. The apparent strike against a Russian-linked military ship – the Sparta 2, one of their notorious military-cargo Sparta fleet – was likely by Ukraine, and either involved a drone launched from another ship, or one flying through Russian territory to the Baltic Sea. Inevitably Russia chose to blame a third option – that Lithuania permitted the drone to fly through its airspace – NATO territory. The accusation feeds the long-standing fiction that Russia is at war with all of NATO. It also raises further the possibility of more Russian malfeasance and sabotage around the Baltics, and the risks of escalation with NATO this carries. The Libya strikes – hitting a Russian naval ship and cargo vessel off the coast of Benghazi, according to Zelensky – further showcases the ability of Kyiv’s drones to embarrass the Kremlin, which had over the last decade paraded its might in Africa, yet whose ships now bring great risk of damage in whichever Mediterranean ports they may dock. The uptick in violence – and where it has spread – was unthinkable five years ago; from being contained inside Ukrainian territory, it spread to Russia in 2024, then to NATO’s eastern borders, with Russia-linked sabotage across the military alliance. The frog is truly boiling, as this war is slowly spreading across the continent, and the months ahead look perilous for two reasons. What a Democratic Congress means for Ukraine Firstly: the Kremlin has a small window before Capitol Hill is taken over by pro-Ukrainian Democrats, and everything from past conduct, to current funding – from Elon Musk to minor Pentagon officials – falls under their scrutiny, if not regulation. The peculiar sympathies with which Donald Trump acts in Russia’s favor will likely be reeled in, in sheer practical terms, and the focus of his inner coterie may turn more to survival under a looming Democratic White House, than their personal priorities when dealing with Putin’s war of choice. Moscow has palpably tried to set the negotiation clock backward, through persuading the US to reframe the talks as about wider “European security infrastructure.” This is something Moscow has long sought, a chance to rewrite the Ukraine conflict as the symptom of NATO’s enlargement eastward. Putin himself has fortified his demands, his most recent appearance in Shenzhen stating Russia had no interest in negotiating a ceasefire – the only real immediate deliverable for diplomacy now. Then he added if the Europeans wanted to join the talks on a technical level (as the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has said the Kremlin had consented to) they should travel to Moscow to make the case to him, and then he’ll think about it. Putin has clearly determined his best negotiating stance is to rip up what’s in front of him, step many paces back, and make any possibility of compromise seem remote. There is a gruesome logic to this: reality is partially on Russia’s side on the battlefield. Capturing the remainder of the Donbas is openly Putin’s main war goal. And while Ukraine has kept Russia from occupying a Donbas town like Kostyantynivka for whole two years, neighboring Kramatorsk and Slavyansk are close to uninhabitable, as Russian drone and airstrikes force civilians out and streets into rubble, ready for the months of gruesome urban warfare ahead. Putin said in Shenzhen that Ukraine’s hold over this remaining 10% of Donbas may slowly become untenable. The horrific cost of Putin’s slow grind forwards, of at least 40,000 dead and injured a month, does come with some tiny results – almost absurd as they are, given the casualties. Perhaps this is the short-term objective the Kremlin sees: make the remainder of Donbas rubble, and then accept a political settlement later, where you can claim victory over the ruins. Disagreement over reality hinders diplomacy But it is the longer term danger that poses the greatest risk to diplomacy. Currently, few of the words spoken by either side relate to each other’s reality. European participation in future multilateral peace summits? Kushner says it’ll happen, the Kremlin says it won’t yet. Territorially, Putin says he controls Kostyantynivka, when he palpably does not. He said Thursday Ukraine started the war, when it did not. Both sides’ demands seem to be moving away from each other. The Kremlin appears to want NATO to fall back and westward, according to some reporting. In turn, some reports suggest Ukraine’s membership of the alliance has even been floated by the US. These are two incompatible red lines. The two sides’ parallel realities are getting further apart, rather than converging on a possible path forward. That is entirely Russia’s intention, and a textbook example of how they use diplomacy to advance their military objectives. But the impact is to create a fictional universe for diplomacy, in which a future restraint of reality on the battlefield becomes elusive. In short: you can’t expect nonsense talks to ever stop the real business of killing. This is where the last year’s mess of failed talks, cosying up to Putin, belittling and bullying Ukraine, European panic and Russian savagery has led the biggest conflict in Europe since the 1940s. A place where Ukrainian drones seem to hit anywhere there’s a Russian ship. Where Russian drones, missiles and helicopters stray monthly into NATO territory without fear of a military retaliation. And where the peace process seems merely a process to please Trump, devoid of actual peace. It is a bleak moment whose only end in sight is the unsettling and even more destabilising collapse of either side.

articles.title: How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth
articles.summary: The US, China and Russia are vying for Africa’s mineral wealth, raising questions about who stands to benefit.
articles.body:
From cobalt mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to lithium deposits in Mali and uranium reserves in Niger, Africa’s mineral wealth is becoming an increasingly important arena of competition between the United States, China and Russia.

China dominates several critical mineral supply chains, while Russia has expanded its influence through security partnerships, particularly in the Sahel. The US, meanwhile, is seeking to secure access to strategic resources through diplomacy, investment and infrastructure projects.

The rivalry extends beyond mining to ports, railways and trade routes connecting Africa’s resources to global markets.

But as foreign powers compete for access, what do African countries stand to gain?

Why are global powers interested in Africa’s minerals?

Africa holds substantial deposits of cobalt, lithium, copper and uranium, resources vital to industries ranging from electric vehicles and renewable energy to advanced technology and defence.

For Washington, securing critical minerals has become a strategic priority amid concerns about dependence on China.

In February, President Donald Trump announced Project Vault, a $12bn initiative to establish a strategic mineral stockpile for US industries.

China has spent years investing in African mining, processing and infrastructure.

Trade between China and Africa reached a record $348bn last year, according to Chinese customs statistics, cementing Beijing’s position as the continent’s largest trading partner.

Russia’s economic footprint is considerably smaller. Moscow has instead relied heavily on military cooperation and security partnerships to expand its influence, particularly in countries that have distanced themselves from Western governments.

Its Africa Corps, established in 2023 under the Russian Ministry of Defence, has taken over much of the Wagner Group’s former operations on the continent.

Gold has also become strategically important to Moscow. A 2024 RAND Europe study commissioned by the United Kingdom’s Foreign Office identified the precious metal as a major feature of Russia’s engagement in Africa.

Why is the DRC central to the competition?

The DRC is the world’s largest producer of mined cobalt, accounting for an estimated 73 percent of global production in 2025, according to the US Geological Survey.

China has established a powerful position in the country’s mining industry, with Chinese companies owning or holding stakes in several major copper and cobalt operations.

Beijing also dominates global cobalt refining, giving it considerable influence over supply chains even when minerals are extracted elsewhere.

Washington is seeking to challenge that position.

Last December, the US and DRC signed a strategic partnership agreement aimed at expanding US access to critical minerals and supporting investment in infrastructure and processing.

Under the agreement, Kinshasa is to identify strategic mining assets and exploration areas, giving American and eligible partner investors rights of first offer on designated projects.

But securing agreements is different from developing mines and processing facilities.

This month, DRC Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba urged Washington to translate the partnership into tangible investments, saying its success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.

Kinshasa wants investment to support domestic mineral processing, electricity access and economic development, rather than simply increasing raw material exports.

Why are transport corridors part of the rivalry?

Control over mineral supply chains depends not only on mines but also on the infrastructure needed to move resources to international markets.

China has made infrastructure investment central to its engagement with Africa through the Belt and Road Initiative, under which dozens of African countries have signed cooperation agreements.

The US, alongside European and African partners, is backing the Lobito Corridor, a transport network linking Angola’s Atlantic coast to the copper and cobalt-producing regions of the DRC, with a planned railway extension into Zambia.

The corridor is intended to provide a more efficient route for mineral exports while strengthening regional trade.

For Washington, it also offers an opportunity to diversify supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese-dominated networks.

For African countries, the project could lower transport costs and attract investment. But its wider benefits will depend on whether it also supports local industries and communities.

Mali and Niger possess significant deposits of lithium, gold and uranium, but political upheaval and armed group activity have complicated foreign investment.

Following military coups and deteriorating relations with Western governments, both countries strengthened security ties with Moscow, as did neighbouring Burkina Faso.

Russia deployed Africa Corps personnel across the region, consolidating its position as a security partner to military-led governments.

Washington is now seeking to rebuild relations.

In February, senior US State Department official Nick Checker visited Mali, signalling a desire to reset ties and reaffirming Washington’s respect for the country’s sovereignty.

The diplomatic outreach comes as foreign companies pursue opportunities in the region’s mining sector.

Mali produced an estimated 9,400 tonnes of lithium last year, according to the US Geological Survey, making it one of Africa’s leading producers.

Chinese interests are involved in the Goulamina lithium mine, while a subsidiary of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom secured an exploration licence for the Bougoula lithium project two years ago.

US commercial interests have also pursued opportunities in Mali’s gold sector.

In neighbouring Niger, uranium has become a focus of renewed US economic engagement following the withdrawal of US troops in 2024.

In September this year, the US International Development Finance Corporation approved financing of up to $414m for the Dasa uranium project, developed by Canadian mining company Global Atomic.

The financing remains subject to conditions, including securing a viable route to transport uranium from the landlocked country.

The project illustrates Washington’s efforts to rebuild economic ties even as Russia maintains a security presence in Niger.

For African governments, growing competition among foreign powers presents opportunities to attract investment, diversify partnerships and negotiate better terms for their mineral resources.

Foreign ownership of mines and processing facilities can leave producing countries dependent on raw material exports, while insecurity, corruption and weak infrastructure can limit the benefits reaching local communities.

The challenge for African governments is to turn international interest into investment that creates jobs, expands domestic processing and strengthens local economies.

As Washington, Beijing and Moscow compete for Africa’s mineral wealth, the real test for African countries may be not which global power wins the race, but how much of the wealth they can retain.
